subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 46-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension returns for follow-up and mentions that a friend recommended an herbal supplement regimen that she wants to start taking, because she "wants to treat the root cause of my stress rather than just take pills."
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "Tell me more about what appeals to you about that approach. Let's go over the known benefits and risks, including possible interactions with your blood pressure medications — and if you'd like, I can refer you to an appropriate complementary medicine provider."
"Herbal supplements are unregulated and largely unproven, so I cannot support that decision if you want to remain my patient."
"Alternative medicine is outside my scope of practice, so you should discontinue your blood pressure medication and follow up with that practitioner instead."
"Plenty of my patients take those supplements without any problems, so go ahead and try whatever you like and let me know how it goes."
"Given the dangers of unproven treatments, if you start this regimen I will need to document nonadherence in your chart and notify the state medical board."

explanation_correct: When a patient wants to try alternative or holistic medicine, the recommended response is to explore the underlying reasons in a supportive, nonjudgmental manner, advise the patient of the known benefits and risks of the treatment — including adverse effects, contraindications, and medication interactions — and consider referral to an appropriate complementary or alternative medicine provider. This keeps the therapeutic relationship intact while ensuring the patient makes an informed decision.

explanation_incorrect.B: This is judgmental and threatening; dismissing the patient's interest risks losing the patient to unmonitored care rather than exploring her reasons and keeping her safe.
explanation_incorrect.C: This is a dismissive referral-out that abandons ongoing medical care and explicitly instructs the patient to stop effective antihypertensive therapy, risking harm.
explanation_incorrect.D: This falsely reassures the patient that supplements are harmless, skipping the required discussion of known benefits, risks, adverse effects, contraindications, and medication interactions.
explanation_incorrect.E: This prematurely invokes authority and punishment; a patient's interest in alternative medicine is not nonadherence or professional misconduct, and this response would destroy trust.

educationalObjective: For a patient interested in alternative or holistic medicine: explore the reasons supportively, discuss known benefits, risks, and drug interactions, and consider referral to an appropriate provider.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: At a 12-month well-child visit, the pediatrician recommends the standard MMR and varicella vaccines. The mother says she has read online that vaccines cause autism, that she "just doesn't trust Big Pharma," and that she wants to delay all immunizations indefinitely. The child is healthy, developmentally normal, and up to date on prior vaccinations.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "The research linking vaccines to autism has been thoroughly discredited, so I'll go ahead and give the vaccines today while she's already here for her checkup."
"As her pediatrician, my duty to protect your child's health overrides parental disagreement, so I am required to notify child protective services today for medical neglect."
"If you won't follow my recommendations, our practice can no longer provide care for your daughter, so you will need to find another pediatrician."

"Tell me more about the concerns you've read about. I can explain the risks and benefits of each vaccine and why they are recommended — but I will not administer routine vaccinations without your consent."
"Millions of children receive these vaccines safely every year, so there is really nothing to worry about — we can simply resume the schedule at her next visit."

explanation_correct: When a parent refuses standard vaccinations for a child, the physician should address the parent's concerns and explain the risks and benefits of vaccination and why the vaccines are recommended, while respecting the parent's authority to consent: routine vaccinations should not be administered without the parent's consent. Maintaining the relationship and providing accurate information is the recommended approach for ongoing counseling.

explanation_incorrect.A: Vaccinating without the parent's consent violates the consent requirement; even with the best interests of the child in mind, routine vaccination requires parental consent.
explanation_incorrect.B: This prematurely invokes authority; vaccine refusal alone is not an indication for child protective services reporting, and the recommended approach is to address concerns and counsel.
explanation_incorrect.C: Dismissing the family from the practice removes the best opportunity to vaccinate the child later and is a coercive, non-patient-centered response rather than addressing the concerns.
explanation_incorrect.E: This falsely reassures the parent and glosses over her specific concerns; without addressing the misinformation, the physician is unlikely to change her decision.

educationalObjective: When a parent refuses standard childhood vaccinations: address the concerns, explain the risks and benefits, and do not administer routine vaccinations without parental consent.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A pharmaceutical representative offers your community clinic a substantial annual sponsorship to fund its hypertension screening program, with the condition that the clinic's physician prominently advertise the company's new antihypertensive drug in patient materials and endorse it in interviews with local media.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "I can accept the sponsorship as long as the money only pays for patient care services and we never let the company choose which clinicians receive it."
"Since it will help my patients, I'll accept the sponsorship and feature your new drug in our materials — a few statements from me on its benefits will only improve their care."
"I cannot take money from industry under any circumstances, so I am also reporting your company to the AMA's ethics committee for offering an improper arrangement to my clinic."
"Let's modify the deal: I'll skip the media interviews, but I can display your drug's logo on our screening flyers while the sponsorship pays my salary supplement."

"I must reject this offer, because sponsorship conditioned on advertising a product creates a conflict of interest — although under the AMA Code of Ethics, gifts that directly benefit patients, special funding for medical education, and independently awarded grants can be acceptable."

explanation_correct: Sponsorship offered in exchange for advertising a specific drug creates a conflict of interest and should be rejected; physicians should generally decline gifts and sponsorships to avoid conflicts of interest. The AMA Code of Ethics does carve out narrow exceptions — gifts that directly benefit patients, special funding for the medical education of students, residents, and fellows, grants whose recipients are chosen by independent institutional criteria, and funds distributed without attribution to sponsors — but none of these applies to an arrangement requiring the physician to advertise and endorse a specific product.

explanation_incorrect.A: This describes parts of the legitimate exceptions but ignores the core condition of this offer: prominent advertising and endorsement of a specific drug, which is disqualifying and creates a conflict of interest.
explanation_incorrect.B: This accepts the arrangement, creating exactly the conflict of interest physicians should decline; a physician's endorsement tied to sponsorship inappropriately promotes a specific product.
explanation_incorrect.C: Refusing industry funds absolutely goes beyond what is required, since the AMA exceptions do permit certain patient-benefiting gifts and educational funding; this response also prematurely invokes an enforcement body for a situation the physician can simply decline.
explanation_incorrect.D: Negotiating the form of the advertisement still ties funding to promotion of a specific drug and adds a personal financial benefit, both of which create a conflict of interest and should be rejected.

educationalObjective: Sponsorship in exchange for advertising a drug should be rejected; AMA exceptions exist only for gifts directly benefiting patients, medical education funding, independently selected grants, and unattributed funds.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 68-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer and worsening pain is admitted for symptom control. After a family meeting, he tells his physician, "I want you to help me end my life. I'm dying anyway, and I don't want to suffer."
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "I'm sorry, but prescribing any medication that might hasten your death is illegal everywhere in the United States, so the only legal option is to continue treatment exactly as it is."

"I understand you're suffering. Although the overwhelming majority of states prohibit physician-assisted dying, I can prescribe medically appropriate analgesics to control your pain, even if they potentially shorten your life."
"I will write you a prescription for a lethal dose of medication so that you can decide when and how to end your suffering — that is what autonomy requires."
"Rather than talking about ending your life, the best thing is hospice; I'm going to arrange the transfer today and we can revisit this if your mood improves."
"I cannot honor that request, and because a patient talking about hastening death is a safety risk, I am contacting psychiatry to evaluate your decision-making capacity involuntarily."

explanation_correct: The appropriate response validates the patient's suffering while giving accurate information: the overwhelming majority of states prohibit most forms of physician-assisted dying, but physicians may prescribe medically appropriate analgesics even if they potentially shorten the patient's life. Aggressive pain control with the intent of relieving suffering is ethically distinct from physician-assisted dying, and offering it respects both autonomy and the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence.

explanation_incorrect.A: This overstates the law: although most states prohibit physician-assisted dying, it incorrectly implies that analgesics that may shorten life are also illegal, which would deny the patient appropriate palliative pain control.
explanation_incorrect.C: This accommodates the request, but physician-assisted dying is prohibited in the overwhelming majority of states; a physician should not prescribe a lethal dose simply because the patient requests it.
explanation_incorrect.D: Transferring to hospice without addressing the request dismisses the patient's concern, and hospice care does not preclude aggressive analgesia; this response also implicitly links the request to mood rather than exploring it.
explanation_incorrect.E: This prematurely invokes coercive measures. A terminally ill patient's request for physician-assisted dying is not an active suicide plan requiring involuntary hospitalization, and this response is not patient-centered or empathetic.

educationalObjective: For a terminally ill patient requesting physician-assisted dying: most states prohibit it, but physicians may prescribe medically appropriate analgesics even if they potentially shorten the patient's life.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 28-year-old woman requests elective tubal sterilization, a nonemergent procedure. Her physician's religious convictions make performing the procedure deeply unacceptable to him. She has already completed thorough counseling and is certain of her decision.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "This procedure is medically unnecessary at your age, so let's talk about why you think you need it instead of scheduling anything."

"I will give you accurate, unbiased information so you can make an informed decision, but I need to tell you that I do not perform this procedure for personal reasons — and I will gladly refer you to a physician who does."
"My personal faith does not permit me to do this, and I believe it would be wrong for you as well; I'd like to discuss alternatives like adoption before you finalize anything."
"I don't perform this procedure, so there is nothing more for us to discuss here — the front desk can give you a list of other practices if you want one."
"Although I have moral objections, your certainty means I'm willing to set them aside and perform the procedure for you myself."

explanation_correct: When a patient requests a nonemergent procedure that is against the physician's personal or religious beliefs, the physician should provide accurate and unbiased information so the patient can make an informed decision, explain in a neutral, nonjudgmental manner that he or she does not perform the procedure, and offer to refer to another physician. This respects both the physician's conscience and the patient's autonomy.

explanation_incorrect.A: This medicalizes a request that has already been considered and dismisses the patient's settled decision instead of providing unbiased information and a referral.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sharing the physician's faith-based view of what would be "wrong for you" is judgmental and attempts to sway the patient's decision, violating the requirement for neutral, nonjudgmental disclosure.
explanation_incorrect.D: Referring out without explanation is dismissive; even with conscientious objection, the physician must still provide accurate information and offer the referral directly.
explanation_incorrect.E: This abandons the physician's stated position under pressure rather than handling it appropriately; the recommended course is honest disclosure plus referral, not performing a procedure that conflicts with one's beliefs.

educationalObjective: For a nonemergent procedure against a physician's personal or religious beliefs: provide accurate unbiased information, explain you do not perform it in a neutral manner, and offer referral.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 54-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has had inadequate response to methotrexate. Her physician recommends adding biologic therapy, but her insurance company has declined to cover the medication because she has not tried a second conventional synthetic DMARD first. She says, "I guess if it's not covered, it's not for me — just tell me what they will pay for."
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "The insurers know what works best, so let's stick to the medications they cover and not complicate things with treatments you cannot afford."
"I'll contact the insurance company and argue with them until they change their decision, and until they do, we should put your treatment plan on hold."

"We should discuss all of your treatment options, including those your insurance does not cover; let me also connect you with our financial assistance programs and the manufacturer's patient-assistance application."
"Honestly, biologics carry serious infection risks, so the denial may be a blessing in disguise — you're better off without that medication anyway."
"You would need to pay out of pocket for that medication, so if you can't afford it, that reflects your own priorities about your health care spending."

explanation_correct: The recommended response is to discuss all treatment options with patients even if some are not covered by their insurance companies, and to inform the patient of financial assistance programs. This acknowledges the obstacle the insurance denial creates rather than letting coverage status dictate the clinical conversation, and it honors the principle of justice by helping the patient access financial assistance.

explanation_incorrect.A: This lets the insurance company's formulary determine which treatments the patient hears about; the physician should discuss all treatment options even when some are not covered.
explanation_incorrect.B: Advocating with the insurer can be appropriate, but suspending the treatment plan until the dispute resolves withholds options from the patient in the meantime and is not the immediate patient-centered response.
explanation_incorrect.D: This falsely reassures the patient by downplaying a biologic's benefits and exaggerating the meaning of the denial; coverage status does not change the medication's clinical role.
explanation_incorrect.E: This frames a financial obstacle as a personal failing and abandons the patient instead of exploring financial assistance programs; it is judgmental rather than helpful.

educationalObjective: When a patient needs a treatment not covered by insurance: discuss all treatment options anyway and inform the patient of financial assistance programs.
